newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: SIA shares firm on listing, India news.
newsitem.headline: SIA shares firm on listing, India news.

text.p: Singapore Airlines shares rose on the local market on Tuesday after the company said it may consider listing some major subsidiaries.
The stock was also bolstered by news from New Delhi that a US$600 million proposal to start air service in India with a local partner had cleared a major government hurdle.
SIA was among the Singapore Stock Exchange's top gainers on Tuesday. SIA Ltd added S$0.20 to S$7.40 by 0937 GMT, while the group's foreign shares rose 40 cents to S$13.20 just before the close.
Analysts said SIA's announcement that it might float units such as Singapore Airport Terminal Services, SIA Engineering and regional carrier SilkAir were positive for the stock.

"In recent years, these subsidiaries have performed well, with pre-tax profit contribution to the group of near $300 million in fiscal year 1996," Nua We Boon, investment analyst with Fraser Securities said.
He said interim results showed they added S$95 million to the group's overall pre-tax profit.
SIA's shares rose early in the day following news it was contemplating listing the subsidiaries.

Demand was spurred further after a senior Indian government official in New Delhi said the Foreign Investment Promotion Board had approved a proposal by SIA and India's Tata Industries Ltd to set up a domestic airline.
The proposal still requires cabinet approval.
An SIA spokesman declined comment on the progress of a venture in which Tata Industries would hold a 60 percent stake and SIA the rest.
Deputy chairman and chief executive Cheong Choong Kong told the airline's in-house magazine that SIA was looking for regional ventures to overcome narrowing profit margins.
"Our current investments in joint ventures are small, but they will grow," Cheong was quoted as saying in the text of an interview made available to Reuters.
He said that as investments multiplied, they would give SIA critical mass to push its rate of return on investments.

"A major solution lies in starting airline-related joint ventures overseas, where the costs are lower, and the growth rates higher because growth is from a lower base, all of which means higher rates of return for the group," Cheong said.
He said a target of 30 percent of group profit from related businesses within 15 years was not inconceivable.

The Indian venture was in line with SIA's efforts to acquire equity in complementary airlines, either to expand its network or to build a secondary hub outside Singapore to accelerate growth, Fraser Securities' Nua said.
